newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Singapore's export slump ending, economists say.
newsitem.headline: Singapore's export slump ending, economists say.

text.p: Singapore is expected to report another fall in exports on Wednesday, showing its economy is still suffering from the recent global slowdown in the electronics industry.
But a Reuters poll of 15 regional financial institutions suggested on Tuesday that the recent slump in the city-state's manufacturing industry may be ending.
The poll, carried out on Monday and Tuesday, produced a forecast of a fall of just 1.4 percent year-on-year in nominal terms in Singapore's non-oil domestic exports in October.
This would be a bounce back from a 6.2 percent fall registered in September and a decline of 6.3 percent in August.
"This month's export figures should herald some recovery in the economy, but the extent of the rebound is extremely difficult to predict," said Tan Min Lan, economist at Merrill Lynch in Singapore.
The was no consensus among economists on the scale of the improvement in exports.

Of the 15 polled, only three economists came up with an identical figure for October -- a fall of two percent -- and estimates ranged from a fall of 5.3 percent year-on-year to a rise of three percent.
Official export figures for October are expected to be released on Wednesday.
Singapore's exports have suffered over the last six months as a result of a slump in the electronics industry in the United States and Japan.
Electronics, computers and related products account for about half the island's total industrial production and almost 60 percent of its non-oil exports.
This dependence helped pull down Singapore's economic growth to a year-on-year rise of just 3.2 percent in the third quarter, from 11.4 percent in the first three months of the year.
But economists say there are now signs of a small recovery in the U.S. electronics industry, which may be beginning to filter through to stronger demand for Singapore exports.

The most recent U.S. semi-conductor book-to-bill ratio, which measures new orders against deliveries in a key electronics market, showed a healthy recovery in demand in October for the first time since the second quarter of the year.
But economists caution it usually takes three to six months for demand in the United States to filter through to demand in the main Asian export markets.
"The recovery is beginning," said Tan. "But it may be the second quarter before we get to the familiar double-digit growth range we are used to seeing in Southeast Asia."

Maminder Singh, economist at Nomura in Singapore, agreed and said there could be a "false dawn" in the first quarter when export growth at the end of 1996 appeared to tail off for a few months after a burst of Christmas demand.
"You may see exports turn down again slightly in the first quarter and it may be well into the second quarter before there is a sustained pick-up," he said.

The same Reuters poll forecast a rise of 1.5 percent year-on-year in Singapore's consumer price index (CPI) of inflation in October. The index rose 1.5 percent year-on-year in September and by 1.4 percent in August.
